name: श्रद्धात्रयविभागयोग
teaching: Your faith is not what you profess — it is what you are: 'a person is made of their śraddhā.' Food, worship, austerity, giving — each splits three ways by the strand behind it, and the same outward act can purify or poison depending on its spirit. The chapter ends with oṁ tat sat: the seal of the real on anything done with faith, and the verdict — asat, nothing — on anything done without it. Faith is not one thing but three, and a person is made of the faith they keep. Food, worship, discipline, and giving each carry the maker's grade — and three syllables, OM TAT SAT, re-address imperfect acts to the Real.
questions: Watch one ordinary choice today — a meal, a gift, a discipline. Which of the three faiths chose it?
Where do you practice austerity for the sake of being seen?
What in your life is done entirely without faith — and is it, as the chapter says, nothing?

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
ये शास्त्रविधिमुत्सृज्य यजन्ते श्रद्धयान्विताः ।
तेषां निष्ठा तु का कृष्ण सत्त्वमाहो रजस्तमः॥
verses.transliteration:
ye śāstravidhimutsṛjya yajante śraddhayānvitāḥ
teṣāṃ niṣṭhā tu kā kṛṣṇa sattvamāho rajastamaḥ
verses.essence: Arjuna asks: those who set aside the ordinances of scripture yet sacrifice filled with faith — what is their standing, Krishna? Sattva, rajas, or tamas?
verses.translation: Those who, setting aside the ordinances of the scriptures, perform sacrifice with faith, what is their condition, O Krishna? Is is Sattva, Rajas or Tamas?

anvaya.parts: शास्त्र (scripture) + विधि (rule): the rule laid down by scripture

anvaya.base: अनु + √इ · to follow; अन्वित · joined with

verses.explanation: Arjuna catches the loose thread of 16.24 at once: scripture is the measure — but what of the millions who worship without ever reading it, full of śraddhā, sincere faith? The grandmother at the village shrine, the devotee of unlettered love. His question is generous and precise, and it opens the Gita's great analysis of faith itself.
verses.connection: Born straight from 16.23–24: where does heartfelt faith stand when the rulebook is absent?
verses.reflection: Honor the unread worshipers in your world today — faith without footnotes still reaches.
verses.background: Chapter 17 opens with Arjuna's question. Krishna has just said that whoever sets aside scripture and acts on desire gains nothing. Arjuna asks about the case that leaves open: people who ignore scripture's rules yet worship with faith. Which of the three qualities of nature (goodness, passion, dullness) do they stand in?
verses.hook: What becomes of people who worship with faith but ignore scripture?

views.text: Takes 'setting aside scripture' to mean people who know no injunction and simply follow the conduct of their elders, not those who knowingly defy it, since real faith could not coexist with such defiance.

Reads niṣṭhā as sthiti, the state one abides in, and says the Lord's answer is meant to show that faith and rites not enjoined by scripture are futile; the threefold division applies to scriptural rites.
Pleads the ordinary person's case: scripture is vast, teachers are rare and life is short, so many worship by copying saints, like a child tracing letters written out for him.
Having heard that disregarding scripture brings no perfection, Arjuna asks about the faith of sincere people who worship without the Vedas, and how it fits the three modes of nature.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
त्रिविधा भवति श्रद्धा देहिनां सा स्वभावजा ।
सात्त्विकी राजसी चैव तामसी चेति तां शृणु॥
verses.transliteration:
trividhā bhavati śraddhā dehināṃ sā svabhāvajā
sāttvikī rājasī caiva tāmasī ceti tāṃ śṛṇu
verses.essence: The Blessed Lord says: threefold is the faith of the embodied, born of their innate nature — sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. Hear of it.
verses.translation: Threefold is the faith of the embodied, which is inherent in their nature the Sattvic (pure), the Rajasic (passionate) and the Tamasic (dark). Do thou hear of it.

anvaya.parts: त्रि (three) + विधा (kind): of three kinds
स्व (own) + भाव (nature) + ज (born): born of one's own nature

verses.explanation: The answer reframes the question: faith is not one thing that people have or lack — it is svabhāva-jā, grown from one's own nature, and it comes in the three colors of everything else. Each person's trust flows along the channel their being has cut. The real question is never *whether* you believe, but what quality of you is doing the believing.
verses.connection: Dissolves the believer/non-believer binary: faith universal, its grade variable — the chapter's thesis.
verses.reflection: Stop asking whether people believe today; ask instead what quality of them is doing the believing.
verses.background: Krishna, the Blessed Lord, answers Arjuna's question. Śrīdhara explains that the faith of those who act from knowing scripture is of one kind, directed to the Supreme, while the faith of those guided only by custom takes three forms; this verse begins the answer by naming them.
verses.hook: Is anyone truly without faith, and where does faith come from?

views.text: Explains svabhāva as the latent impressions of past-life acts that surface at death; sattvic faith turns to the gods, rajasic to yakṣas and rākṣasas, tamasic to ghosts and goblins.
Defines faith as eagerness for a means believed to win one's goal; it follows one's ruci, the taste formed by vāsanās, which in turn come from contact with the guṇas of body and senses.

A person whose heart is made tender by abundant sattva acts with scriptural authority whatever he does, while one stained by rajas or tamas misses the spirit of scripture even while following its rules.

Those who act from knowing scripture have a single sattvic faith aimed at the Lord; only people acting by mere custom have faith split three ways, lacking the discernment that could reshape their nature.
No one lacks faith; unbelievers place it in their senses, intellect or scientific theories, which also need a leap of faith. Faith takes three forms according to one's nature.

verses.devanagari:
सत्त्वानुरूपा सर्वस्य श्रद्धा भवति भारत ।
श्रद्धामयोऽयं पुरुषो यो यच्छ्रद्धः स एव सः॥
verses.transliteration:
sattvānurūpā sarvasya śraddhā bhavati bhārata
śraddhāmayo'yaṃ puruṣo yo yacchraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ
verses.essence: The faith of each is according to their essential nature, Bharata. A person is made of faith: whatever one's faith is, that very thing one is.
verses.translation: The faith of each is in accordance with his nature, O Arjuna. The man consists of his faith; as a man's faith is, so is he.

anvaya.meaning: in keeping with one's inner being
anvaya.parts: सत्त्व (inner being, mind) + अनुरूप (conforming): conforming to one's mind
श्रद्धा (faith) + मय (made of): consisting of faith
यद् (which) + श्रद्धा (faith): one whose faith is in that which

verses.explanation: One of the Gita's most quoted axioms: śraddhāmayo 'yaṁ puruṣaḥ — a human being is made of faith. First the ground: sattvānurūpā, each person's faith conforms to their inner make-up, a mind shaped by past impressions. Then the turn: yo yac-chraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ — as one's faith is, so one is. We are built around what we rely on: whatever you bank on when no one is watching — money, status, method, God — that reliance is your actual religion and your actual self. Identity lives not in beliefs professed but in reliance practiced. Show me your faith and I have met you.
verses.connection: The chapter's center of gravity: identity defined by the direction of trust.
verses.reflection: Run the axiom on yourself tonight: what I rely on when no one watches — that is my faith, and my self.
verses.background: Krishna has said faith is threefold and born of nature. Śrīdhara raises an objection: Krishna elsewhere, speaking to Uddhava, counted faith as a mark of goodness alone, so how can it be threefold? This verse answers by tying each person's faith to the quality of their own mind.
verses.hook: Why does what you believe in shape who you become?

views.text: Takes sattva as the internal organ stamped with past impressions; since a person is shaped by faith, his standing in sattva, rajas or tamas can be inferred from what he worships.
A person is a transformation of his faith: faith in auspicious acts brings their fruit, so what one attains follows chiefly from what one has faith in.
Answers an objection that faith is purely sattvic: sattva itself varies by degree and is mixed with rajas and tamas in people, so the faith that follows it is threefold too.
Where we place our faith, in money, fame, values or God, directs the whole course of our life. The quality of that faith is in turn shaped by the nature of our mind.

verses.devanagari:
यजन्ते सात्त्विका देवान्यक्षरक्षांसि राजसाः ।
प्रेतान्भूतगणांश्चान्ये यजन्ते तामसा जनाः॥
verses.transliteration:
yajante sāttvikā devānyakṣarakṣāṃsi rājasāḥ
pretānbhūtagaṇāṃścānye yajante tāmasā janāḥ
verses.essence: Sattvic people worship the gods; the rajasic worship yakshas and rakshasas; the others — tamasic people — worship ghosts and hosts of spirits.
verses.translation: The Sattvic or the pure men worship the gods; the Rajasic or the passionate worship the Yakshas and the Rakshasas; the others (the Tamasic or the deluded people) worship the ghosts and the hosts of the nature-spirits.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative plural (subject)

anvaya.parts: यक्ष (yaksha, wealth-spirit) + रक्षस् (rakshasa, demon): yakshas and rakshasas, a pair listed together

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative plural (subject)

anvaya.parts: भूत (spirit, being) + गण (host): hosts of spirits

verses.explanation: The first diagnostic: read a person's altar. Clarity bows to the luminous; restless ambition courts powers that grant and threaten — yakshas of wealth, rakshasas of force; darkness gravitates to the shadowy and the dead. Worship is a mirror before it is a door: each nature kneels to a magnified image of itself.
verses.connection: First application of 17.3: the chosen deity as a portrait of the chooser.
verses.reflection: Read one altar today — yours or another's — as a mirror of the worshiper.
verses.background: Having said that a person is made of their faith, Krishna now shows how the three kinds of faith are told apart by their effects. Śrīdhara introduces it this way: the beings one chooses to worship reveal which quality one's faith belongs to.
verses.hook: What kinds of beings do people of each temperament worship?

views.text: Counts the Seven Mothers among the hosts of spirits, and remarks that only one in thousands is established in sattva; most creatures are rooted deep in rajas or tamas.
Grades the fruits: sattvic worship of the gods brings joy unmixed with pain, rajasic worship limited joy mixed with pain, tamasic joy so slight it borders on pain.
Each class worships deities of its own nature, so a worshipper's guṇa can be read from the deity he likes to worship.
Like attracts like: the tamasic turn to ghosts, the rajasic to powerful and wrathful beings, the sattvic to celestial gods. Worship is perfectly directed only when offered to God himself.

verses.devanagari:
अशास्त्रविहितं घोरं तप्यन्ते ये तपो जनाः ।
दम्भाहंकारसंयुक्ताः कामरागबलान्विताः॥
verses.transliteration:
aśāstravihitaṃ ghoraṃ tapyante ye tapo janāḥ
dambhāhaṃkārasaṃyuktāḥ kāmarāgabalānvitāḥ
verses.essence: Those who perform terrible austerities not ordained by scripture, yoked to hypocrisy and egoism, driven by the force of desire and passion —
verses.translation: Those men who practise terrific austerities not enjoined by the scriptures, given to hypocrisy and egoism, impelled by the force of lust and attachment.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + शास्त्र (scripture) + विहित (ordained): not ordained by scripture
दम्भ (hypocrisy) + अहंकार (ego) + संयुक्त (joined): joined with hypocrisy and ego

anvaya.meaning: driven by desire, attachment and force
anvaya.parts: काम (desire) + राग (attachment) + बल (force) + अन्वित (endowed): impelled by the force of desire and attachment

verses.explanation: Now the dark twin of Arjuna's question: not the rule-less worship of simple faith, but ghora tapas — ferocious self-mortification outside all guidance, powered by dambha and ahaṅkāra. Austerity can be ego's most convincing disguise: the spectacular fast, the public ordeal, suffering performed as superiority. Intensity, the Gita warns, is not the same as depth.
verses.connection: Distinguishes 17.1's innocent faith from its counterfeit: violence dressed as discipline.
verses.reflection: Distrust spectacular self-denial today, in yourself first — intensity is not depth.
verses.background: Śrīdhara says Krishna now adds a further case among the passionate and the dull: the most unfortunate, who follow custom and false teachers into fierce austerities scripture never prescribes. This verse describes them; its sentence ends in 17.6.
verses.hook: Are harsh, self-imposed austerities a sign of real spiritual strength?

views.text: Such austerity causes pain to oneself and to other creatures; kāma-rāga can also be read as desired objects and the longing to enjoy them.
These are the most unfortunate, who copy heretics by blind imitation; bala here means stubborn insistence, and the sentence completes in the next verse's 'know them of demonic resolve'.
Describes mortification done to attract people and money, such as standing on one leg; bodily torture is not real tapas and brings no liberation.
Lying on thorns or fasting to wither the body shows conviction but lacks knowledge. Such faith is in the mode of ignorance and runs against the path the scriptures recommend.

verses.devanagari:
कर्षयन्तः शरीरस्थं भूतग्राममचेतसः ।
मां चैवान्तःशरीरस्थं तान्विद्ध्यासुरनिश्चयान्॥
verses.transliteration:
karṣayantaḥ śarīrasthaṃ bhūtagrāmamacetasaḥ
māṃ caivāntaḥśarīrasthaṃ tānviddhyāsuraniścayān
verses.essence: — senselessly torturing the assembled elements in the body, and me too, dwelling within the body: know them to be of demonic resolve.
verses.translation: Senseless, torturing all the elements in the body and Me also, Who dwell in the body, know thou these to be of demonical resolves.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative plural (while tormenting)

anvaya.parts: शरीर (body) + स्थ (standing in): situated in the body
भूत (element) + ग्राम (collection): the collection of elements
अ (without) + चेतस् (mind): lacking discernment
अन्तर् (within) + शरीर (body) + स्थ (dwelling): dwelling within the body
आसुर (demonic) + निश्चय (resolve): those whose resolve is demonic

verses.explanation: The verdict carries a startling tenderness toward flesh: the bhūta-grāma, the whole assembly of elements and organs that make up the body, is not raw material for ordeals — and brutalizing it torments mām caiva, 'me as well,' the indweller of 15.15. The body is not the soul's enemy but God's address. Self-violence, however piously framed, is vandalism of a temple from the inside.
verses.connection: Extends 16.18's insight inward: harming one's own body is also striking the resident Lord.
verses.reflection: Treat the body as a temple in your care today: feed it, rest it, and torment no part of it.
verses.background: This verse finishes the sentence begun in 17.5 about those who practise fierce austerities scripture does not prescribe. Having named their hypocrisy and desire, Krishna now says what their practice does to the body and to him within it, and gives his verdict.
verses.hook: Whom do people harm when they torture their own bodies for religion?

views.text: 'Tormenting Me' means simply disregarding My injunctions; the Lord sits in the body as witness of its acts and thoughts. Such people are named so that they can be avoided.
They torture the elements of the body and the individual self, which is part of the Lord; acting against His commands, they gain no joy and fall into calamity.
The aggregate is the earth and other elements that build the body, wasted by pointless fasts; the Lord dwells within as inner controller and is hurt by the breach of His command.
Those who abuse their bodies in the name of austerity disrespect the Supreme Soul who lives within. Their resolve, however intense, is demoniac and contrary to scripture.

verses.devanagari:
आहारस्त्वपि सर्वस्य त्रिविधो भवति प्रियः ।
यज्ञस्तपस्तथा दानं तेषां भेदमिमं शृणु॥
verses.transliteration:
āhārastvapi sarvasya trividho bhavati priyaḥ
yajñastapastathā dānaṃ teṣāṃ bhedamimaṃ śṛṇu
verses.essence: Even the food dear to each is of three kinds, as are sacrifice, austerity and charity. Hear now the distinction between them.
verses.translation: The food also which is dear to each is threefold, as also sacrifice, austerity and almsgiving. Hear thou the distinction of these.

anvaya.parts: त्रि (three) + विध (kind): of three kinds

verses.explanation: The analysis goes domestic: four arenas — food, worship, discipline, giving — each refracted into three. Note the diagnostic key: priyaḥ, what is *dear* to each. Not what you eat under duress but what you crave reveals the strand in charge. The Gita is about to read the soul from the dinner plate — the most everyday spiritual audit in scripture.
verses.connection: Table of contents for 17.8–22: the three gunas traced through plate, altar, practice, and purse.
verses.reflection: Let today's audit start at the plate: what is dear to me reveals which strand is ordering.
verses.background: The question of 17.1 has been answered through the objects of worship. Śrīdhara says Krishna now shows the three qualities in food, sacrifice, austerity and giving as well, over thirteen verses, so that one may grow in goodness by choosing its forms. This verse announces the four topics.
verses.hook: Do your food, sacrifices, austerities and gifts reflect your nature?

refs.note: The coarsest part of food leaves the body, a subtler part becomes flesh, and the subtlest becomes mind, so food shapes our nature.
By eating pure food, the mind becomes pure, linking diet to inner purity.

views.text: The food dear to all who eat it is of three kinds, as are sacrifice, austerity and charity; the Lord asks Arjuna to listen to the classification about to be given.
The distinctions are taught for a practical end: to strive for growth in sattva by giving up rajasic and tamasic food, sacrifice and the rest and taking up the sattvic.
You can learn your own temperament from the foods you crave; since the body is the horse that carries one to liberation, it should be built from pure, wholesome food.
Mind and body influence each other, so what we eat shapes our nature and our nature shapes what we prefer. Pure minds choose pure foods.

verses.devanagari:
आयुःसत्त्वबलारोग्यसुखप्रीतिविवर्धनाः ।
रस्याः स्निग्धाः स्थिरा हृद्या आहाराः सात्त्विकप्रियाः॥
verses.transliteration:
āyuḥsattvabalārogyasukhaprītivivardhanāḥ
rasyāḥ snigdhāḥ sthirā hṛdyā āhārāḥ sāttvikapriyāḥ
verses.essence: Foods that increase life, vitality, strength, health, happiness and delight — savory, rich, substantial and agreeable to the heart — are dear to the sattvic.
verses.translation: The foods which increase life, purity, strength, health, joy and cheerfulness (good appetite), which are savoury and oleaginous, substantial and agreeable, are dear to the Sattvic (pure) people.

anvaya.meaning: increasing life, vigour, strength, health, happiness, delight
anvaya.parts: आयुस् (life) + सत्त्व (vigour) + बल (strength) + आरोग्य (health) + सुख (happiness) + प्रीति (delight) + विवर्धन (increasing): that increase all these

anvaya.base: √स्निह् · to be oily; स्निग्ध · oily, rich

anvaya.parts: सात्त्विक (sattvic person) + प्रिय (dear): dear to the sattvic

verses.explanation: Sattvic eating defined by its aftermath: six increases — lifespan, clarity, strength, health, ease, even prīti, simple delight. The food itself: rasya, full of natural flavor; snigdha, gently rich; sthira, sustaining; hṛdya, kind to the heart. Nothing puritan here — pleasure is on the list — only the question every appetite should be asked: what does this leave behind in me?
verses.connection: First plate: nourishment measured by what it builds, not how loudly it tastes.
verses.reflection: Choose one meal today by its aftermath — what it builds in you — and still let it delight.
verses.background: The account of the three kinds of food begins, one verse each. Krishna first names the foods dear to people of goodness (sattva, the clear and balanced quality), described by what they do for the eater and by their taste.
verses.hook: Which foods nourish life, strength and a calm, happy mind?

views.text: Sattvic food augments life, firmness of mind (sattva), strength, health and delight; it is succulent, oleaginous, substantial in that it lasts long in the body, and agreeable to one's liking.
Takes sattva here as knowledge, since sattva gives rise to knowledge (14.17); such food fosters understanding, and hṛdya means beautiful to look at.
Glosses sattva as zest (utsāha) and prīti as relish; sthira means food whose essence stays long in the body, and hṛdya food that wins the heart at first sight.
Prīti means good appetite without nausea; names milk, butter, fresh fruit, almonds and barley as sattvic and says the mind is formed from the subtle part of food.
Sattvic foods are juicy, naturally tasty and wholesome, such as grains, pulses, fruits, vegetables and milk. A vegetarian diet supports the goodness that helps spiritual life.

verses.devanagari:
कट्वम्ललवणात्युष्णतीक्ष्णरूक्षविदाहिनः ।
आहारा राजसस्येष्टा दुःखशोकामयप्रदाः॥
verses.transliteration:
kaṭvamlalavaṇātyuṣṇatīkṣṇarūkṣavidāhinaḥ
āhārā rājasasyeṣṭā duḥkhaśokāmayapradāḥ
verses.essence: Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, harsh and burning — causing pain, grief and sickness — are coveted by the rajasic.
verses.translation: The foods that are bitter, sour, saline, excessively hot, pungent, dry and burning, are liked by the Rajasic and are productive of pain, grief and disease.

anvaya.meaning: bitter, sour, salty, very hot, sharp, dry, burning
anvaya.parts: कटु (bitter, pungent) + अम्ल (sour) + लवण (salty) + अति (very) + उष्ण (hot) + तीक्ष्ण (sharp) + रूक्ष (dry) + विदाहिन् (burning): a list of qualities of the food

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, genitive singular (of/to)

anvaya.parts: दुःख (pain) + शोक (grief) + आमय (disease) + प्रद (giving): that cause pain, grief and disease

verses.explanation: The rajasic plate: everything turned up — ati-uṣṇa, *excessively* hot, sharp, scouring. Stimulation mistaken for satisfaction: food chosen to jolt rather than nourish, because the restless strand needs each meal to be an event. The bill arrives in three installments: duḥkha now, śoka after, āmaya — illness — on credit.
verses.connection: Second plate: intensity-seeking at the table, and its deferred invoice.
verses.reflection: Notice the craving for jolt over nourishment once today — and turn one dial down from 'event' to 'meal.'
verses.background: After the foods of goodness, Krishna turns to those liked by people of passion (rajas, the restless, driven quality). Śrīdhara notes that the word "excessively" applies to every taste in the list.
verses.hook: What kind of food do restless, passionate people crave?

views.text: Reads 'very' with every item — very bitter, very sour and so on — and explains the grief as distress at not getting the food one craves.
Dry foods are those that leave the eater parched, burning foods those that cause a burning sensation; such foods promote pain, sorrow and disease.
Also applies 'ati' to all seven, with examples like neem, pepper and mustard; duḥkha is the immediate burning, śoka the later dejection, āmaya disease.
Food overloaded with chili, salt or sugar becomes rajasic and brings illness and agitation. Eating is for health, not for the palate, so the wise choose sattvic food.

verses.devanagari:
यातयामं गतरसं पूति पर्युषितं च यत् ।
उच्छिष्टमपि चामेध्यं भोजनं तामसप्रियम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yātayāmaṃ gatarasaṃ pūti paryuṣitaṃ ca yat
ucchiṣṭamapi cāmedhyaṃ bhojanaṃ tāmasapriyam
verses.essence: That which is stale, tasteless, foul-smelling, left overnight, the leavings of others and unfit for offering — such food is dear to the tamasic.
verses.translation: That which is stale, tasteless, putrid, rotten, refuse and impure, is the food liked by the Tamasic.

anvaya.parts: यात (gone) + याम (a three-hour watch): food kept past a watch, gone cold
गत (gone) + रस (flavour, essence): whose essence is gone

anvaya.base: परि + √वस् · to stay; पर्युषित · left overnight

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + मेध्य (fit for sacrifice): unfit for offering
तामस (tamasic person) + प्रिय (dear): dear to the tamasic

verses.explanation: The tamasic plate: yāta-yāmam, food whose hour has passed — life-force departed, only bulk remaining. The deeper note is indifference: eating as mere stuffing, without care for freshness, source, or sanctity (amedhyam — unfit even to offer). Where rajas over-attends to food and sattva attends rightly, tamas has stopped attending at all.
verses.connection: Third plate completes the food-mirror: appetite as a window into care itself.
verses.reflection: Refuse the food of indifference today — the stale, the careless — attention is the first ingredient.
verses.background: The third and last kind of food: what people of dullness (tamas, the heavy, inert quality) prefer. After the nourishing foods of goodness and the burning foods of passion, Krishna names food that is stale, spoiled or left over.
verses.hook: Which foods are dear to those in dullness and ignorance?

refs.note: The word for meat is explained as 'the one I eat here will eat me hereafter', showing the karmic debt of meat-eating.

views.text: Renders yātayāma as 'not properly cooked' rather than 'stale', so that it does not repeat gatarasa, which already means food that has lost its essence.
Amedhya is food unfit to be offered in worship, so it can never become sacred leftovers; anyone who cares for their welfare should grow sattva by eating sattvic food.
Yātayāma is cooked rice gone cold after a watch, paryuṣita food cooked the day before, ucchiṣṭa what others have left after eating.
Stale food kept over three hours, foul food and meat belong to ignorance. The human body is built for plant food, and meat-eating also creates bad karma.

verses.devanagari:
अफलाकाङ्क्षिभिर्यज्ञो विधिदृष्टो य इज्यते ।
यष्टव्यमेवेति मनः समाधाय स सात्त्विकः॥
verses.transliteration:
aphalākāṅkṣibhiryajño vidhidṛṣṭo ya ijyate
yaṣṭavyameveti manaḥ samādhāya sa sāttvikaḥ
verses.essence: Sacrifice offered according to rule by those desiring no fruit, with mind composed in the conviction 'offering is simply to be made' — that is sattvic.
verses.translation: That sacrifice which is offered by men without desire for reward as enjoined by the ordinance (scripture), with a firm faith that to do so is a duty, is Sattvic or pure.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + फल (fruit) + आकाङ्क्षिन् (desiring): by those who desire no fruit
विधि (rule, injunction) + दृष्ट (seen): as laid down by injunction

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is done)
gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (must be done)

verses.explanation: Sattvic worship in one phrase: yaṣṭavyam eva — 'this is to be offered,' full stop. No transaction pending, no invoice attached; the act complete in itself, like a sunrise. Mind samādhāya, gathered and settled. This is the niṣkāma-karma of chapter 2 at the altar: worship as pure expression, not negotiation.
verses.connection: Worship enters the triage: the sattvic offering asks nothing back.
verses.reflection: Do one act today with the clean grammar: it is simply to be offered — no invoice attached.
verses.background: With food done, Krishna turns to the second of the four topics announced in 17.7, sacrifice. Śrīdhara notes that its three kinds take three verses, and this one gives the sacrifice of goodness first.
verses.hook: What makes an offering pure rather than a bargain?

views.text: 'It must simply be offered' means doing the rite exactly as it should be done, with the firm thought that no human goal is to be gained by it.
The sacrifice is offered for its own sake as worship of the Lord, with the right hymns, materials and rites that scripture enjoins.
Yajña is not only ritual: any unselfish act done without egoism or expectation of reward, offered to the Lord, is a sacrifice and purifies the mind.
Sacrifice in goodness is done by scriptural rule, with no wish for reward, purely because it is due as worship of the Lord.

verses.devanagari:
अभिसन्धाय तु फलं दम्भार्थमपि चैव यत् ।
इज्यते भरतश्रेष्ठ तं यज्ञं विद्धि राजसम्॥
verses.transliteration:
abhisandhāya tu phalaṃ dambhārthamapi caiva yat
ijyate bharataśreṣṭha taṃ yajñaṃ viddhi rājasam
verses.essence: But that which is offered with the fruit in view, and for the sake of display — know that sacrifice, best of Bharatas, to be rajasic.
verses.translation: The sacrifice which is offered, O Arjuna, seeking a reward and for ostentation, know thou that to be a Rajasic Yajna.

anvaya.form: compound used as adverb (for the sake of)
anvaya.parts: दम्भ (show) + अर्थ (purpose): for the sake of display

anvaya.form: pronoun, neuter, nominative singular (agrees loosely with the sacrifice)
verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is done)

anvaya.parts: भरत (Bharata) + श्रेष्ठ (best): best among the Bharatas

verses.explanation: Two motives, often braided: abhisandhāya phalam, the worship-as-investment, divine favor expected on schedule; and dambhārtham, the ritual as theater, performed toward the human audience as much as heaven. The act may be liturgically perfect — the strand is read from the *aim*, never the choreography.
verses.connection: Rajasic worship: the altar as marketplace and stage at once — echoing 16.17's name-only rites.
verses.reflection: Catch worship performing for two audiences today — heaven and the neighbors — and dismiss one.
verses.background: The second kind of sacrifice, after the one offered without desire for its fruit in 17.11. Krishna now describes the rite of passion, which Śrīdhara glosses as performed to advertise one's own greatness.
verses.hook: What turns a sacrifice into a business deal with God?

views.text: Sacrifice performed with a result in view, or else for ostentation, should be known as done through rajas.
Display means the intention 'let the world take me to be this kind of person': the rite is aimed at one's own image in others' eyes.
The motive may be heaven, a son, wealth or fame, or showing oneself off as pious and learned; such a performer has no aspiration for knowledge of the Self.
Even a grand ceremony becomes rajasic when the motive is 'what will I get', such as prestige. Pure devotion seeks nothing in return.

verses.devanagari:
विधिहीनमसृष्टान्नं मन्त्रहीनमदक्षिणम् ।
श्रद्धाविरहितं यज्ञं तामसं परिचक्षते॥
verses.transliteration:
vidhihīnamasṛṣṭānnaṃ mantrahīnamadakṣiṇam
śraddhāvirahitaṃ yajñaṃ tāmasaṃ paricakṣate
verses.essence: Sacrifice devoid of rule, without food offered, without mantra, without gifts, empty of faith — that they declare tamasic.
verses.translation: They declare that sacrifice to be Tamasic which is contrary to the ordinances of the scriptures, in which no food is distributed, which is devoid of Mantras, gifts and faith.

anvaya.parts: विधि (rule) + हीन (lacking): without scriptural direction

anvaya.base: असृष्टान्न · where food is not given out
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + सृष्ट (given out) + अन्न (food): one in which food is not distributed
मन्त्र (sacred formula) + हीन (lacking): without mantras
अ (without) + दक्षिणा (fee to officiants): with no gift to the priests
श्रद्धा (faith) + विरहित (bereft of): bereft of faith

verses.explanation: Tamasic worship defined by five absences: no order, no shared food, no sacred word, no honorarium to the officiant, and the void at the center — śraddhā-virahitam, faith itself missing. Ritual as empty husk, gone through because it was always gone through. The form survives the spirit's departure the way a shell outlasts the snail.
verses.connection: Completes the worship-triad: from selfless offering, to transaction, to hollow motion.
verses.reflection: Find any hollow ritual you still run — motions outliving meaning — and either refill it or retire it.
verses.background: The third and last kind of sacrifice, that of dullness. After rites done as duty and rites done for reward and show, Krishna lists what this one lacks; Śrīdhara notes that "they declare" refers to the learned.
verses.hook: What does a sacrifice look like when it lacks faith and order?

views.text: Asṛṣṭānna means food not distributed to Brāhmaṇas, and 'without mantras' also covers faults of intonation and pronunciation.
Vidhi-hīna means lacking the direction of learned, virtuous Brāhmaṇas who say 'perform this'; asṛṣṭānna means using materials scripture does not sanction.
Scripture settles what is right when people disagree. Rituals that ignore its rules, share no food and honour no priests, done out of laziness or defiance, show faithlessness.

verses.devanagari:
देवद्विजगुरुप्राज्ञपूजनं शौचमार्जवम् ।
ब्रह्मचर्यमहिंसा च शारीरं तप उच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
devadvijaguruprājñapūjanaṃ śaucamārjavam
brahmacaryamahiṃsā ca śārīraṃ tapa ucyate
verses.essence: Worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers and the wise; purity, uprightness, continence and harmlessness — this is called austerity of the body.
verses.translation: Worship of the gods, the twice-born, the teachers and the wise, purity, straightforwardness, celibacy and non-injury are called the austerities of the body.

anvaya.meaning: worship of gods, twice-born, teachers, the wise
anvaya.parts: देव (god) + द्विज (twice-born) + गुरु (teacher) + प्राज्ञ (wise one) + पूजन (worship): worship of these four
ब्रह्मन् (the sacred) + चर्य (conduct): the student's life of continence
अ (not) + हिंसा (harming): not harming

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is said)

verses.explanation: The redefinition of tapas begins — and the body's austerity contains no ordeal at all: reverence rightly placed, cleanliness, uprightness, continence, harmlessness. After 17.5's self-torturers, the correction is pointed: true discipline of the body is not what you inflict on it but how it carries you through the world — whom it bows to, what it refrains from harming.
verses.connection: First panel of the tapas-triptych (17.14–16): austerity rebuilt as conduct, not ordeal.
verses.reflection: Practice body-tapas the true way today: bow rightly, stay clean, harm nothing — no ordeal required.
verses.background: The third topic of 17.7 is austerity (tapas, disciplined practice). Śrīdhara says that before grading it by the three qualities, Krishna first divides austerity by its instrument: body, speech and mind. This verse gives austerity of the body.
verses.hook: What does disciplining the body look like in daily life?

refs.note: Without purifying the body through austerity one cannot reach the final state of yoga, as gold is purified in fire.

views.text: Bodily austerity is done by the whole group of body and organs in which the body predominates, pointing ahead to the five causes of action in 18.15.
Purity means bathing in sacred waters, uprightness means bodily action matching the mind, and continence means not looking on women as objects of pleasure.
The wise are named apart from teachers because wisdom is not bound to caste, as Vidura shows; brahmacarya means control, not suppression, of the sex-force.
Austerity, like fire purifying gold, transforms life from mundane to divine. Bodily austerity means serving the pure, restraining the senses, keeping clean and simple, and not hurting others.

verses.devanagari:
अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत् ।
स्वाध्यायाभ्यसनं चैव वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
anudvegakaraṃ vākyaṃ satyaṃ priyahitaṃ ca yat
svādhyāyābhyasanaṃ caiva vāṅmayaṃ tapa ucyate
verses.essence: Speech that causes no agitation, truthful, pleasant and beneficial; and the regular practice of sacred recitation — this is called austerity of speech.
verses.translation: Speech which causes no excitement, truthful, pleasant and beneficial, the practice of the study of the Vedas, are called austerity of speech.

anvaya.parts: अन् (not) + उद्वेग (agitation, fear) + कर (causing): that causes no distress
प्रिय (pleasant) + हित (beneficial): both pleasant and beneficial
स्वाध्याय (recitation of scripture) + अभ्यसन (practice): regular study of scripture
वाच् (speech) + मय (made of): consisting of speech

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is said)

verses.explanation: Perhaps the most practical verse in the Gita: four tests for every sentence — anudvega-karam, does it disturb no one? satyam, is it true? priyam, is it kind? hitam, does it help? Śaṅkara insists all four must hold together: speech missing even one is not austerity. Truth alone does not pass; truth weaponized fails the discipline. To pass all four gates, day after day, is a tapas more demanding than any fast — and svādhyāyābhyasanam, the steady practice of sacred recitation, keeps the tongue in training.
verses.connection: Second panel: the fiercest austerity relocated to the smallest muscle.
verses.reflection: Pass every sentence through the four gates today: does it disturb? is it true? kind? helpful?
verses.background: The second of the three kinds of austerity by instrument. After austerity of the body in 17.14, Krishna describes the austerity carried out through speech.
verses.hook: What does disciplined, wholesome speech sound like?

refs.note: Speak truth pleasantly, never hurtful truth or pleasant falsehood; this is the eternal dharma behind the austerity of speech.

views.text: The 'and' binds the four qualities: speech that is true but hurtful, or pleasant but untrue, is not austerity. His model is 'Be calm, my boy; practise study and yoga, and you will gain the highest.'
'True' is explained by what follows: pleasant when heard and beneficial later; merely reporting what actually happened is not what 'speaking the truth' means here.
Cites Manu: speak what is true and pleasant; do not speak an unpleasant truth or a pleasant falsehood. Control of speech is hard but needed for peace.
Austerity of speech is truthful, inoffensive, pleasing and beneficial words, along with recitation of the Vedas.

verses.devanagari:
मनः प्रसादः सौम्यत्वं मौनमात्मविनिग्रहः ।
भावसंशुद्धिरित्येतत्तपो मानसमुच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
manaḥ prasādaḥ saumyatvaṃ maunamātmavinigrahaḥ
bhāvasaṃśuddhirityetattapo mānasamucyate
verses.essence: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, purity of feeling — this is called austerity of the mind.
verses.translation: Serenity of mind, good-heartedness, self-control, purity of nature this is called mental austerity.

anvaya.parts: मनस् (mind) + प्रसाद (clarity): a clear, calm mind
आत्मन् (self, mind) + विनिग्रह (restraint): restraint of the mind
भाव (motive, feeling) + संशुद्धि (purity): purity of intention

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is said)

verses.explanation: The innermost panel: manaḥ-prasāda, a mind kept clear like settled water; saumyatvam, moonlike mildness; mauna — not merely a closed mouth but the quiet *behind* thought; and the summit, bhāva-saṁśuddhi, the scrubbing of motive itself. The triptych completes a ladder inward: easy to police the hands, harder the tongue, hardest the silent intention no one else will ever audit.
verses.connection: Third panel: tapas at its root — where only the practitioner and the indweller can inspect.
verses.reflection: Take the inmost austerity for an hour: a settled mind, a mild manner, and one motive scrubbed clean.
verses.background: The third kind of austerity by instrument. After body and speech, Krishna names the austerity of the mind, completing the threefold practice he is about to grade by the three qualities.
verses.hook: How do you practise discipline of the mind itself?

views.text: Mauna here means control of the mind, the cause named by its effect; ātma-vinigraha is withdrawal of the mind in general, and bhāva-saṃśuddhi is freedom from trickery in dealing with others.
Serenity is freedom from anger; saumyatva is the mind turned to others' good; purity of mind is not thinking of anything other than the self.
Mauna is the state of a muni, that is, reflection (manana), and self-restraint is withdrawing the mind from sense-objects.

Mental austerity is highest, since a mastered mind masters body and speech. Like a garden, the mind must be planted with noble thoughts and weeded of resentment, for thought by thought we shape our destiny.

verses.devanagari:
श्रद्धया परया तप्तं तपस्तत्त्रिविधं नरैः ।
अफलाकाङ्क्षिभिर्युक्तैः सात्त्विकं परिचक्षते॥
verses.transliteration:
śraddhayā parayā taptaṃ tapastattrividhaṃ naraiḥ
aphalākāṅkṣibhiryuktaiḥ sāttvikaṃ paricakṣate
verses.essence: This threefold austerity, practiced with supreme faith by those disciplined and desiring no fruit — that they call sattvic.
verses.translation: This threefold austerity, practised by steadfast men, with the utmost faith, desiring no reward, they call Sattvic.

anvaya.parts: त्रि (three) + विध (kind): of three kinds
अ (not) + फल (fruit) + आकाङ्क्षिन् (desiring): by those who desire no fruit

verses.explanation: The grading rubric applied to tapas: the full triptych — body, speech, mind — practiced śraddhayā parayā, with the highest faith, and signed with the now-familiar signature: aphalākāṅkṣibhiḥ, no fruit demanded. Discipline as devotion's posture rather than ambition's tool. The same fast, the same silence, can be any of the three strands; the faith and the aim decide.
verses.connection: Grades 17.14–16: the threefold practice turned sattvic by faith without bargain.
verses.reflection: Practice all three quietly today — body, speech, mind — wanting nothing back, and call it sattvic.
verses.background: Austerity of body, speech and mind has been described. Śrīdhara says Krishna now shows that this threefold austerity is itself of three kinds, in three verses; this verse describes it when practised in goodness.
verses.hook: When is austerity truly pure?

views.text: Supreme faith means belief in God and in the world hereafter, and yukta means self-controlled; the 'they' who call it sattvic are the noble.
Yukta means imbued with the thought that this threefold practice of body, speech and mind is worship of the Supreme Person.
All three kinds of austerity involve faith: the sattvic person's faith is in the austerity itself, the rajasic's in show, the tamasic's in ruining others.
Austerity in goodness is done selflessly, seeking no material benefit, with faith that stays firm in success and failure and practice that never lapses through laziness.

verses.devanagari:
सत्कारमानपूजार्थं तपो दम्भेन चैव यत् ।
क्रियते तदिह प्रोक्तं राजसं चलमध्रुवम्॥
verses.transliteration:
satkāramānapūjārthaṃ tapo dambhena caiva yat
kriyate tadiha proktaṃ rājasaṃ calamadhruvam
verses.essence: Austerity practiced for honor, respect and reverence, and with ostentation — that is called rajasic here: unstable and impermanent.
verses.translation: The austerity which is practised with the object of gaining good reception, honour and worship, and with hypocrisy, is here said to be Rajasic, unstable and transitory.

anvaya.form: compound used as adverb (for the sake of)
anvaya.parts: सत्कार (respect) + मान (honour) + पूजा (worship) + अर्थ (sake): for the sake of being respected, honoured and worshipped

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is done)

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + ध्रुव (fixed, lasting): impermanent

verses.explanation: Rajasic tapas: discipline performed toward an audience — satkāra, māna, pūjā: the welcome, the title, the deference. Its verdict is structural, not moral: calam adhruvam, unstable — because practice powered by applause stops when the applause does. What is done to be seen lasts exactly as long as the seeing.
verses.connection: The performative twin of 17.12's showy sacrifice: discipline with a gallery.
verses.reflection: Notice where your discipline performs for applause — and do that practice once today in secret.
verses.background: After the austerity of goodness, practised with faith and no wish for reward, Krishna describes austerity practised in passion. Śrīdhara spells out the honour it seeks: being praised as a true ascetic, people rising and bowing, gifts of wealth.
verses.hook: Why is austerity done for honour and fame unstable?

views.text: Satkāra is being praised as 'a pious Brāhmaṇa given to austerity'; iha means its fruit comes only in this world, and calam means its result is unpredictable.
It is unsteady because its rewards, like heaven, are temporary and bring the fear of falling, and impermanent because they are bound to perish.
Austerity done for fame is worse than useless; it is dropped half-done as soon as it is seen to bring no gain.
Austerity is a tool of purification, but done for respect, power or praise it becomes rajasic, a material motive dressed in spiritual means.

verses.devanagari:
मूढग्राहेणात्मनो यत्पीडया क्रियते तपः ।
परस्योत्सादनार्थं वा तत्तामसमुदाहृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
mūḍhagrāheṇātmano yatpīḍayā kriyate tapaḥ
parasyotsādanārthaṃ vā tattāmasamudāhṛtam
verses.essence: Austerity practiced with deluded obstinacy, with self-torture, or for the sake of destroying another — that is declared tamasic.
verses.translation: That austerity which is practised out of a foolish notion, with self-torture, or for the purpose of destroying another, is declared to be Tamasic.

anvaya.parts: मूढ (deluded) + ग्राह (grip, insistence): with a deluded fixation

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is done)
compound used as adverb (for the sake of)
anvaya.parts: उत्सादन (destruction) + अर्थ (purpose): for destroying

verses.explanation: The darkest tapas: mūḍha-grāheṇa, gripped by a deluded fixation — discipline as self-punishment, or worse, parasyotsādanārtham, austerity wielded as a weapon, power accumulated to destroy. The epics are full of such figures: ascetics whose mountains of practice fund a single curse. Spiritual force, the verse warns, takes the moral shape of its wielder.
verses.connection: Closes the tapas-triad where 17.5–6 began: the ordeal that wounds self or other.
verses.reflection: Check that no practice of yours punishes you or aims at another — force is not the fruit.
verses.background: The last of the three grades of austerity, that of dullness. After austerity done for its own sake and austerity done for honour, Krishna names austerity driven by delusion; Śrīdhara notes that harming another here means sorcery aimed at ruin.
verses.hook: What is austerity like when it hurts oneself or others?

views.text: Austerity undertaken with a foolish intent, a conviction born of non-discrimination, whether it pains one's own body or aims at destroying another, is said to be born of tamas.
Deluded people, lacking right understanding, practise from obstinate determination, torturing themselves without regard to their own capacity, or to cause suffering to others.
Austerity 'for another's ruin' is abhicāra, a rite performed to destroy someone; the obstinacy springs from lack of discernment.
Lists ordeals such as hooks in the flesh, hanging head-down over fire and the five-fire penance, and says none of them leads to knowledge of the Self.
Confused people torture themselves or injure others in the name of austerity, ignoring scripture and the body's limits. It achieves nothing and only deepens bodily consciousness.

verses.devanagari:
दातव्यमिति यद्दानं दीयतेऽनुपकारिणे ।
देशे काले च पात्रे च तद्दानं सात्त्विकं स्मृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
dātavyamiti yaddānaṃ dīyate'nupakāriṇe
deśe kāle ca pātre ca taddānaṃ sāttvikaṃ smṛtam
verses.essence: The gift given with the thought 'it is simply to be given' — to one who can make no return, in fit place and time, to a worthy person — that gift is held to be sattvic.
verses.translation: That gift which is given to one who does nothing in return, knowing it to be a duty to give in a fit place and time to a worthy person, that gift is held to be Sattvic.

anvaya.form: gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (must be done)
verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is given)

anvaya.base: अनुपकारिन् · one who does no favour in return
anvaya.parts: अन् (not) + उपकारिन् (one who helps back): one who does no service in return

anvaya.form: past participle, neuter, nominative singular (is regarded)

verses.explanation: The final arena: giving. Sattvic charity carries the chapter's signature phrase — dātavyam iti, 'it is to be given,' duty's clean grammar — and one piercing qualifier: anupakāriṇe, to one who *cannot reciprocate*. The gift escapes the economy entirely; no return possible, none imagined. Then the craft: right place, right time, right hands — generosity with its eyes open.
verses.connection: The purse examined: sattvic giving as the exit from exchange itself.
verses.reflection: Give once today where no return is possible — anupakarine — right time, right place, open hand.
verses.background: Krishna has finished grading austerity by the three qualities and takes up the last of his four topics, giving. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as the threefold division of the gift promised earlier (at 17.7); Krishna begins with the gift of goodness.
verses.hook: When is a gift given in the purest way?

refs.note: In the age of Kali, charity is the means of purification, underlining the duty to give.
Of dharma's four tenets, giving in charity by any means is the chief in the age of Kali.
Give one-tenth of rightly earned wealth in charity as a duty, dedicated to the pleasure of God.

views.text: The gift goes to one who will not serve in return, though even one who can is not excluded; right place is a holy site like Kurukṣetra, right time a Saṅkrānti, the right person one versed in the Vedas.
Pātre is locative to match 'place' and 'time'; or it can be read as a dative of pātṛ, protector, since a worthy recipient protects the giver from all misfortune.
The gift should go to one who cannot return it or from whom no return is expected, and the donor should not boast of his charity.
Giving is a duty that loosens attachment, expands the heart and builds compassion. Charity is sattvic when given freely from the heart to worthy recipients at the right time and place.

verses.devanagari:
यत्तु प्रत्युपकारार्थं फलमुद्दिश्य वा पुनः ।
दीयते च परिक्लिष्टं तद्दानं राजसं स्मृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yattu pratyupakārārthaṃ phalamuddiśya vā punaḥ
dīyate ca parikliṣṭaṃ taddānaṃ rājasaṃ smṛtam
verses.essence: But that which is given expecting a return, or with the fruit in view, or given grudgingly — that gift is held to be rajasic.
verses.translation: And, that gift which is given with a view to receive something in return, or looking for a reward, or reluctantly, is held to be Rajasic.

anvaya.form: compound used as adverb (for the sake of)
anvaya.parts: प्रति (back) + उपकार (favour) + अर्थ (purpose): to get a favour back

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is given)
past participle used as adverb (with distress)
past participle, neuter, nominative singular (is regarded)

verses.explanation: Rajasic giving: the gift as opening move — pratyupakāra, the favor that books a favor; or merit banked toward heaven's ledger; or parikliṣṭam, the rupee released with a wince. The hand opens but the fist remains inside it. Such giving binds giver and receiver in a web of accounts where sattvic giving had cut both free.
verses.connection: The transactional middle: generosity still inside the marketplace of 17.12.
verses.reflection: Catch the gift with a hook in it today — the favor that books a favor — and unhook one.
verses.background: Krishna continues the three kinds of giving. After the gift of goodness, given with no thought of return, he now describes the second kind, the gift of passion.
verses.hook: What spoils a gift given with strings attached?

views.text: Three marks: giving so that the receiver will serve one later, giving for an unseen reward that will accrue to oneself, and giving with reluctance.
Adds a mark of its own: giving useless things grudgingly, with a sly expectation of getting something back.
Giving to a holy man in the hope of washing away one's sins is also rajasic, as is grieving at heart after making the gift.
The best giving is unasked, the next is glad giving on request. Giving reluctantly, or regretting the amount afterward, is charity in the mode of passion.

अदेशकाले यद्दानमपात्रेभ्यश्च दीयते ।
असत्कृतमवज्ञातं तत्तामसमुदाहृतम्॥

asatkṛtamavajñātaṃ tattāmasamudāhṛtam

verses.translation: The gift that is given at a wrong place and time, to unworthy persons, without respect or with insult is declared to be Tamasic.

verses.explanation: Tamasic giving wounds while it gives: wrong moment, wrong hands, and the manner that poisons the matter — asatkṛtam avajñātam, tossed without respect, given *down*. A coin flung with contempt takes more than it leaves. The triad complete, the lesson across all three: in giving, the how and the why outweigh the what.
verses.connection: Completes the four-arena audit (food, worship, tapas, dana) — and 17.23 turns to the syllables that purify all of them.
verses.reflection: Mind the manner of one giving today: the how can wound or bless more than the what.
verses.background: Krishna gives the third and last kind of gift, the one marked by dullness. With it, his survey of food, sacrifice, austerity and giving by the three qualities is complete.
verses.hook: When does giving to others do harm instead of good?

views.text: A wrong place is an unholy one crowded with the impure; a wrong time is one not known for merit, unlike Saṅkrānti. Even at the right place and time, a gift without kind words, foot-washing and honour is tamasic.

The wrong time is a period of ritual impurity (aśauca), and the unworthy are rakes, actors and dancers. Even when place, time and recipient are right, giving stripped of the customary honours, or with scorn, stays tamasic.

These restrictions are not a reason to withhold alms from the poor and needy; for them they do not apply. The fault lies in a donor who gives without good faith, offers no seat and treats the recipient with contempt.
Charity without thought for place, time, person or attitude serves no purpose. Giving money to one who misuses it makes the giver share in the resulting wrong.

verses.devanagari:
ॐतत्सदिति निर्देशो ब्रह्मणस्त्रिविधः स्मृतः ।
ब्राह्मणास्तेन वेदाश्च यज्ञाश्च विहिताः पुरा॥
verses.transliteration:
oṃ tatsaditi nirdeśo brahmaṇastrividhaḥ smṛtaḥ
brāhmaṇāstena vedāśca yajñāśca vihitāḥ purā
verses.essence: 'OM TAT SAT' — this is recorded as the threefold designation of Brahman. By this were ordained of old the brahmanas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices.
verses.translation: "Om Tat Sat": This has been declared to be the triple designation of Brahman. By that were created formerly, the Brahmanas, the Vedas and the sacrifices.

anvaya.form: present participle of √अस् used as a name, neuter (the word 'Sat')

anvaya.base: ब्रह्मन् · Brahman, the Absolute (also the Veda)

anvaya.parts: त्रि (three) + विधा (kind): having three kinds

verses.explanation: After all the grading, the remedy: three syllables that consecrate. OM — the primal sound; TAT — 'That,' the pointing beyond; SAT — 'the Real, the Good.' The triple name of Brahman, older than the rites themselves, offered now as a seal: whatever imperfection clings to our mixed-strand offerings, these sounds re-address the package to the Absolute.
verses.connection: Opens the chapter's coda (17.23–28): the mantra that lifts imperfect acts toward the Real.
verses.reflection: Seal one act today with the three syllables — OM TAT SAT — and feel it re-addressed to the Real.
verses.background: Every act has now been graded, and a worry follows: by this measure most sacrifice, austerity and giving fall short, so why make the effort? Śrīdhara introduces the verse as the remedy, a way to make even such acts good, and Krishna begins with the threefold name of the Absolute.
verses.hook: What three words point to the Absolute itself?

views.text: The knowers of Brahman in the Vedānta regard Om, Tat and Sat as Brahman's triple name. Saying brahmins, Vedas and sacrifices were made by it praises the name, and uttering it corrects a defect in a rite.
'Brahman' here means the Veda, especially its ritual part. Om is spoken at the start of every Vedic recitation, while Tat and Sat mark the rites as worthy of honour.
Answers a worry: if nearly all sacrifice, gift and austerity turn out rajasic or tamasic, is the effort wasted? No: this threefold name can make even a deficient act complete.
Even goodness lies within Maya and should be a stepping-stone, not a resting place. Moving beyond the three modes, Om Tat Sat names aspects of the Absolute Truth.

verses.devanagari:
तस्मादोमित्युदाहृत्य यज्ञदानतपःक्रियाः ।
प्रवर्तन्ते विधानोक्ताः सततं ब्रह्मवादिनाम्॥
verses.transliteration:
tasmādomityudāhṛtya yajñadānatapaḥkriyāḥ
pravartante vidhānoktāḥ satataṃ brahmavādinām
verses.essence: Therefore, with the utterance of 'OM', the acts of sacrifice, charity and austerity prescribed by scripture are always begun by the expounders of Brahman.
verses.translation: Therefore, with the utterance of "Om" are the acts of sacrifice, gift and austerity as enjoined in the scriptures, always begun by the students of Brahman.

anvaya.form: pronoun, ablative singular, used as an adverb (therefore)

anvaya.base: ॐ · the sacred syllable, name of Brahman

anvaya.meaning: acts of sacrifice, gift and austerity
anvaya.parts: यज्ञ (sacrifice) + दान (gift) + तपस् (austerity) + क्रिया (act): the acts that consist of these three
विधान (injunction) + उक्त (stated): stated in the injunctions

anvaya.meaning: of the expounders of the Veda
anvaya.base: ब्रह्मवादिन् · one who expounds the Veda
anvaya.parts: ब्रह्म (Veda, Brahman) + वादिन् (one who speaks of): those who teach the Veda

verses.explanation: OM in practice: the opening syllable, sounded before every sacred act like a key turned before a journey. Its function is orientational — one breath that gathers the scattered doer and points the deed toward its source. Millennia of practice stand behind the instruction: begin in the sound, and the act begins in the sacred.
verses.connection: First syllable applied: OM as the doorway every consecrated act walks through.
verses.reflection: Begin one undertaking today with OM — a single breath that points the deed at its source.
verses.background: Having named the threefold designation, OM TAT SAT, Krishna takes the three words one at a time to show the worth of each. He starts with OM, the first of the three, and those who teach the Veda.
verses.hook: Why do the wise begin sacred acts by uttering Om?

views.text: Therefore those who study and expound the Vedas always begin the scripturally prescribed acts of sacrifice, charity and austerity after uttering the syllable Om.
Because the Vedas are always recited after Om, 'expounders of the Veda' covers everyone of the three stations who learns the Vedas and performs their rites, not only learned teachers.
Since the designation is so praised, acts begun with Om go on fully even when some part of the rite is missing; they become complete.
Om at the start of an act is like a walking stick on a hill or a boat on a river. The point is not to renounce sacrifice and charity but to perform them with total surrender to God.
Om represents the formless aspect of God and is the primordial sound in creation. It begins many Vedic mantras as a seed sound to invoke auspiciousness.

verses.devanagari:
तदित्यनभिसन्धाय फलं यज्ञतपःक्रियाः ।
दानक्रियाश्च विविधाः क्रियन्ते मोक्षकाङ्क्षिभिः॥
verses.transliteration:
tadityanabhisandhāya phalaṃ yajñatapaḥkriyāḥ
dānakriyāśca vividhāḥ kriyante mokṣakāṅkṣibhiḥ
verses.essence: With 'TAT' — without aiming at the fruit — the acts of sacrifice and austerity and the manifold acts of charity are performed by the seekers of liberation.
verses.translation: Uttering Tat, without aiming at the fruits, are the acts of sacrifice and austerity and the various acts of gifts performed by the seekers of liberation.

anvaya.form: pronoun used as a name, neuter (the word 'Tat')

anvaya.base: अभि + सम् + √धा · to aim at, intend
anvaya.form: gerund with negative prefix (without having aimed at)

anvaya.parts: यज्ञ (sacrifice) + तपस् (austerity) + क्रिया (act): acts of sacrifice and austerity
दान (gift) + क्रिया (act): acts of charity

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person plural (are done)

anvaya.parts: मोक्ष (liberation) + काङ्क्षिन् (one who longs for): one who longs for liberation

verses.explanation: TAT — 'That' — the most self-effacing word in language: pure reference away from oneself. Acting in its spirit, the mokṣa-kāṅkṣī releases the fruit at the moment of acting: this deed belongs to *That*, not to my account. One syllable performing the whole renunciation of 2.47 — the gift dissolved into the boundless the instant it leaves the hand.
verses.connection: Second syllable: TAT as the act's release into the Absolute — niskama karma in a single word.
verses.reflection: Say TAT inwardly as you finish one task: this belongs to That — and release it from your ledger.
verses.background: After OM, Krishna turns to the second word of the formula, TAT, 'That', and describes its place in the acts of those who seek freedom.
verses.hook: What does saying 'Tat' express about the purpose of an offering?

views.text: Tat is a name of Brahman. After uttering it, seekers of Liberation perform sacrifice, austerity and varied charity, such as gifts of land and gold, without regard for the results.
The acts themselves are designated 'Tat': study, sacrifice and gifts done without aiming at results, by those seeking only release, are means to Brahman, and Tat is a recognised name of Brahman.
The name Tat is praised because acts done with it purify the mind and make one drop the intent on fruit, so they produce the longing for liberation itself.
Uttering Tat is like saying 'these are not mine': what was begun with Om is handed over to Brahman with Tat, freeing the doer from egoism and the bondage of action.
All fruits of action belong to God. Chanting Tat with sacrifice, austerity and charity shows they are offered not for reward but for the soul's welfare through God-realization.

verses.devanagari:
सद्भावे साधुभावे च सदित्येतत्प्रयुज्यते ।
प्रशस्ते कर्मणि तथा सच्छब्दः पार्थ युज्यते॥

sadbhāve sādhubhāve ca sadityetatprayujyate
praśaste karmaṇi tathā sacchabdaḥ pārtha yujyate
verses.essence: 'SAT' is used in the sense of reality and in the sense of goodness; likewise, Partha, the word 'SAT' is applied to any praiseworthy act.
verses.translation: The word Sat is used in the sense of reality and of goodness; and so also, O Arjuna, the word Sat is used in the sense of an auspicious act.

verses.explanation: SAT carries a double load no translation holds at once: the *real* (sad-bhāva) and the *good* (sādhu-bhāva) — one word insisting that being and goodness are finally the same fact. Whatever is praiseworthy partakes of reality; evil, by this grammar, is a kind of unrealness. To act well is to be more real.
verses.connection: Third syllable unpacked: the metaphysics hidden in calling something 'sat'.
verses.reflection: Practice SAT both ways today: be more real by doing one unarguably good thing.
verses.background: The third word, SAT, gets two verses. In this first one Krishna sets out what the word means in ordinary use, before tying it in the next verse to the practice of sacrifice, austerity and giving.
verses.hook: What does the word 'Sat' mean when applied to people and deeds?

refs.note: A prayer to the Lord as the truth in creation, maintenance and dissolution, the source and essence of all truth, showing the depth of the word Sat.

views.text: Sad-bhāva is the coming into being of what was not there, like the birth of a son; sādhu-bhāva is a person of bad conduct becoming good. Sat is also said of an auspicious rite such as a marriage.
The word Sat has power to make a defective action complete: when one flaw threatens to render a good act asat, uttering Sat removes the defect and brings it to success.
Sat has many senses: lasting goodness and virtue, auspicious sacred acts, and that which always exists, the eternal truth.

verses.devanagari:
यज्ञे तपसि दाने च स्थितिः सदिति चोच्यते ।
कर्म चैव तदर्थीयं सदित्येवाभिधीयते॥
verses.transliteration:
yajñe tapasi dāne ca sthitiḥ saditi cocyate
karma caiva tadarthīyaṃ sadityevābhidhīyate
verses.essence: Steadfastness in sacrifice, in austerity and in charity is also called 'SAT'; and action for the sake of That is likewise designated 'SAT'.
verses.translation: Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity and gift, is also called 'Sat' and also action in connection with these (or for the sake of the Supreme) is called 'Sat'.

verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is called)

verses.explanation: SAT extended from word to way of life: sthiti, the *staying* — showing up for the discipline again this week, this year — is itself the Real in action; and tad-arthīyam, anything whatsoever done for That's sake, earns the name. The sacred stops being a category of special acts and becomes a direction any act can face.
verses.connection: SAT made practical: constancy and God-ward intent as reality's own signature on a life.
verses.reflection: Let constancy be your offering today — showing up again is itself called SAT.
verses.background: Continuing his account of SAT, Krishna moves from the word's everyday senses (existence, goodness, an auspicious rite) to the one who practises. Śaṅkara sums up the point of the three names: used with faith, they make even acts lacking goodness good.
verses.hook: Why is steadiness in sacrifice and charity also called 'Sat'?

refs.note: A prayer to the Lord as the truth in creation, maintenance and dissolution, the source and essence of all truth, showing the depth of the word Sat.

views.text: Tad-arthīyam means action meant for sacrifice, gift and austerity, or for God whose names are being discussed. Used with faith, the three names make even acts lacking sattva good and sattvic.
Om, Tat and Sat each turn an act toward Brahman. Tat, a general pronoun that names no particular thing, signals the absence of intent for any particular fruit; Sat means praise.
Action whose aim is the Supreme includes worship offerings and sweeping and decorating the shrine courtyard, and even remoter work such as earning money for them; all of it is called sat.
Steadfast sacrifice, austerity and charity, and work done for God, are called Sat because they connect us to the Supreme Truth, the eternal and good.

verses.devanagari:
अश्रद्धया हुतं दत्तं तपस्तप्तं कृतं च यत् ।
असदित्युच्यते पार्थ न च तत्प्रेत्य नो इह॥
verses.transliteration:
aśraddhayā hutaṃ dattaṃ tapastaptaṃ kṛtaṃ ca yat
asadityucyate pārtha na ca tatpretya no iha
verses.essence: Whatever is offered, given or practiced without faith is called 'asat', Partha — it is nothing hereafter, and nothing here.
verses.translation: Whatever is sacrificed, given or performed, and whatever austerity is practised without faith, it is called 'Asat', O Arjuna; it is naught here or hereafter (after death).

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + श्रद्धा (faith): absence of faith

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular

verses.explanation: The chapter's last word answers its first question by inversion: Arjuna asked about faith without scripture; the close addresses *works* without faith, and the verdict is annihilating: asat, unreal. Whatever is offered, given or practiced aśraddhayā, without faith, however grand, counts for nothing: na ca tat pretya no iha, not hereafter and not here. The whole chapter compresses to this: śraddhā is the substance; act, scale and form are only the container. A torrent of faithless religion sums to zero on both ledgers, while 9.26's single leaf, offered with love, counts in full.
verses.connection: Seals the faith-chapter: forms without faith are nothing — the perfect threshold to ch18's question of renouncing forms themselves.
verses.reflection: Check the substance, not the container, tonight: whatever lacked faith today counted nowhere — refill it.
verses.background: The chapter began with Arjuna asking about faith (17.1), and it closes on faith here. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as a warning meant to make every act be done with faith: Krishna names what becomes of acts done without it.
verses.hook: What comes of rituals and gifts done without faith?

views.text: Faithless acts are asat because they stand outside the discipline that leads to the Lord. However much effort they cost, they bring no result after death and no credit here, since the wise condemn them.
Even acts the śāstra enjoins become asat, without power, when done without faith: they lead neither to release nor to any desired result within saṃsāra.
Asat here does not mean non-existent but that which changes and leaves no lasting benefit. Faithless rites are like rain on rock or ghee poured on cold ashes.
Acts done without faith in scripture are imperfect and bear good fruit neither here nor hereafter. Faith should rest not on one's own mind but on the scriptures and the Guru.
